Thomas Gray was so self-critical he famously published only 13 poems in his life. He wasn't known for his ODES, his most famous poem being "Elegy written in a Country Churchyard" --- has some really lovely lines, the beginning sets the tone:

The curfew tolls the knell of parting day,
         The lowing herd wind slowly o'er the lea,
The plowman homeward plods his weary way,
         And leaves the world to darkness and to me.

Now fades the glimm'ring landscape on the sight,
         And all the air a solemn stillness holds,
Save where the beetle wheels his droning flight,
         And drowsy tinklings lull the distant folds...

***

Gray contemplates how just as the liveliness of the day fades into the stillness of evening, so too do all of us come to an end, no matter what we've done or who we were:

Some village-Hampden, that with dauntless breast
         The little tyrant of his fields withstood;
Some mute inglorious Milton here may rest,
         Some Cromwell guiltless of his country's blood.

Then he contemplates how he'll be remembered, and how nature can "teach the rustic moralist to die,"

There at the foot of yonder nodding beech
         That wreathes its old fantastic roots so high,
His listless length at noontide would he stretch,
         And pore upon the brook that babbles by.

Arguably, one of our greatest evolutionary advantages has been our knack for pattern recognition. Besides seeing scenes from the Iliad in clouds and stained ceilings, many of us find that every crossword puzzle finds itself woven into our life somehow, right? *Right?*

I’ve been bingeing V. S. Naipaul lately. I’d only read some short stories of his in college and so I missed the next 25 years of his later literary output. And I’m in love—I’m so in love. But I digress. In ‘Half a Life,’ one of Naipaul’s characters, a provincial editor attending a gathering of glamorous expatriates who, he says, have been leading “glittering lives,” quotes this line from Gray’s Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard: “Perhaps in this neglected spot is laid some heart once pregnant with celestial fire.” I’ve been rereading the rest of the poem since. 

I flew home Wednesday, and today (almost yesterday now), I went to see my mom, whom I lost not long ago. She’s not resting in a neglected spot, exactly, but it is fall: That feeling of the world curling up to go to sleep is there in the mellow colors and the swirling leaves. 

I don’t want to wax lyrical; I did that before I finally walked back to my car. Besides Gray’s words speak more vividly than mine can. I just wanted to say that 275 years later, on a different continent, there are still quiet, somber places that strike one as so at odds with the once-fiery hearts secreted beneath them.
